articles.title: The Night a Few Words Put Out a Fire
articles.dek: In 1993 a single assassination nearly set South Africa ablaze. What Nelson Mandela said next shows what James meant about the small spark and the small rudder.
articles.quote: The tongue that can set a forest burning can also steer a ship home, when the wisdom that comes from heaven has its hand on the rudder.
articles.illustration: Mandela's address after Chris Hani's assassination
articles.body:
On the morning of April 10, 1993, the Saturday of the Easter weekend, Chris Hani pulled into the driveway of his home in Dawn Park, east of Johannesburg. He had only gone out to buy the newspaper. Hani was one of the most loved leaders in Black South Africa, a hero to millions of young people in the townships, and his country was in the fragile middle of talks to end apartheid. As he stepped out of his car, a man walked up and shot him at close range. Hani died on his own driveway, a few steps from his front door.

Across the street, a white neighbour named Retha Harmse saw a car speeding away. She was an Afrikaner, from the very community many Black South Africans had learned to fear, and she did something simple and brave. She wrote down the licence plate and called the police. Within hours they had arrested the gunman, a far-right immigrant from Poland. By then, though, the country was already smouldering. Anger rose across the townships like heat off a tin roof at noon, and many people believed that the long-feared civil war had finally arrived.

Nelson Mandela was not yet president. He was a former prisoner of twenty-seven years who led the African National Congress, and in those tense days he went on national television. He could have poured fuel on the fire, and few would have blamed him. Instead he said, "Tonight I am reaching out to every single South African, black and white, from the very depths of my being." Then he spoke the sentence historians still quote: "A white man, full of prejudice and hate, came to our country and committed a deed so foul that our whole nation now teeters on the brink of disaster. A white woman, of Afrikaner origin, risked her life so that we may know, and bring to justice, this assassin." In one breath he placed a white woman beside the grieving Black majority as someone to honour. There were still marches and painful clashes in the days that followed, yet the war did not come. Within months, negotiators fixed the date of South Africa's first free election, and in April 1994 people of every colour stood in the same long lines to vote.

Filipinos understand the power of a few words more than most. We have watched one careless message in the family group chat end years of closeness between cousins. This very month, after the barangay elections, neighbours who campaigned against each other must still share the same street, the same sari-sari store and the same Sunday Mass, and a single remark over the fence can either heal the wound or keep it open for a generation. The apostle James wrote a whole chapter about this.

James was the brother of Jesus and the respected leader of the church in Jerusalem. He wrote to Jewish believers "scattered among the nations" (James 1:1), small house churches under pressure, where members argued, played favourites with the rich, and were quick to speak and slow to listen (James 1:19). In the synagogue culture they came from, being a teacher carried great honour, and many wanted the title. So James opens chapter three with a warning: "Not many of you should become teachers, my fellow believers, because you know that we who teach will be judged more strictly" (James 3:1). Then he admits something humbling about himself and everyone else: "We all stumble in many ways" (James 3:2).

What follows is one of the most vivid passages in the New Testament. James reaches for pictures every listener knew. "When we put bits into the mouths of horses to make them obey us, we can turn the whole animal" (James 3:3). He points to the great grain ships that crossed the Mediterranean, driven by fierce winds yet "steered by a very small rudder wherever the pilot wants to go" (James 3:4). Then comes the picture that would have made his first readers wince, because they lived in dry hill country where a summer brush fire could race across a whole valley in an afternoon.

"Likewise, the tongue is a small part of the body, but it makes great boasts. Consider what a great forest is set on fire by a small spark." (James 3:5)

The Greek of that last sentence carries a lovely piece of wordplay. James uses the same word, hēlikos, twice in a row. It is a word of measure that can mean "how small" or "how great" depending on the context, so the line reads almost like "what-size a fire, what-size a forest." The word itself shows that the size of a spark tells you nothing about the size of what it can do. James goes on to call the tongue "a fire, a world of evil" (James 3:6), and he concludes with honest realism that "no human being can tame the tongue" (James 3:8).

Many readers stop there and walk away discouraged. Yet James's first two pictures carry a hopeful note that is easy to miss. A bit and a rudder are instruments of control. They exist to bring a powerful horse safely home and to bring a heavy ship into harbour "wherever the pilot wants to go." One way to read the passage is that James is describing a tool of enormous steering power, which can wreck or rescue depending on whose hand is on it. The small spark and the small rudder are the same size. In Mandela's speech, the words that could have burned a nation became the rudder that turned it toward an election.

So who holds the rudder, if no human can tame the tongue? James answers in the second half of the chapter. He sets two kinds of wisdom side by side. One is earthly, full of "bitter envy and selfish ambition" (James 3:14). The other is "the wisdom that comes from heaven," which "is first of all pure; then peace-loving, considerate, submissive, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial and sincere" (James 3:17). The taming of the tongue happens from above, as a gift, as we ask God for wisdom, and James had already promised that God "gives generously to all without finding fault" (James 1:5).

James also names the deepest reason our words matter. "With the tongue we praise our Lord and Father, and with it we curse human beings, who have been made in God's likeness" (James 3:9). Every person we speak about carries the image of God, including the person who voted for the other candidate and the relative who hurt us at the reunion. This was the quiet genius of Mandela's words. In the hour when it would have been easiest to curse a whole group, he found the face of God's image on the other side of the line and spoke it aloud. A white Afrikaner woman's courage became the cold water poured on a burning field. As James asks, "Can both fresh water and salt water flow from the same spring?" (James 3:11).

You may never address a nation, but this week you will speak into a kitchen, an office, a group chat or a barangay hall. Before you answer the person who has wounded you, you can pause long enough to pray for heaven's wisdom, and then look for your own "Retha Harmse" in the situation: the true and good thing on the other side that you can honestly name. Saying that one good thing out loud is often the turn of the rudder that brings everyone home.

James ends the chapter with a farmer's promise: "Peacemakers who sow in peace reap a harvest of righteousness" (James 3:18). The tongue that can set a forest burning can also steer a ship home, when the wisdom that comes from heaven has its hand on the rudder. Your words today may feel small, and they are. Small words, offered to God, have turned whole nations, and they can certainly turn a family, a friendship or a street toward peace.

articles.title: The Bread No One Brought Him
articles.dek: On the night his wife died, God told Ezekiel to refuse the food and comfort his neighbors would bring. That hard command shows how much it means to grieve with someone.
articles.quote: Grief was never meant to be carried alone, and a plate of pancit carried to a neighbor's lamay is a small, holy way of saying so.
articles.body:
On the third night of a lamay in a narrow street in Marikina, the tarpaulin tent still covers half the road, and the monobloc chairs have not moved since Tuesday. Someone has plugged a thermos into an extension cord that snakes out of the sari-sari store on the corner. A neighbor from two houses down arrives straight from her shift with a tray of pancit, sets it beside the guest book, and squeezes the widow's hand without saying a word. Near the gate a few cousins deal another round of cards, and they will keep dealing until the sky turns grey, because in our culture a grieving family is never left alone with its dead through the night.

Anyone who has sat through a Filipino wake knows how much of it is food and presence. There is the envelope of abuloy slipped quietly into the box, the coffee and biscuits that appear from nowhere, and the tita who washes every cup before she goes home. None of it undoes the loss, yet all of it tells the family that they still belong to someone. We call this pakikiramay, from the root damay, which means to share in another person's suffering. It is one of the kindest instincts our people carry, and it opens a door into one of the hardest passages in the whole Bible.

The prophet Ezekiel was a priest who had been carried off to Babylon in 597 BC with the first wave of captives from Judah. He lived among the exiles beside the Kebar canal, and for years he had warned them that Jerusalem would fall. They did not believe him. As long as the temple stood in Jerusalem, they reasoned, God would never let the city go. Chapter 24 opens on the very day the Babylonian army began its siege of Jerusalem (Ezekiel 24:1–2). Hundreds of miles away, with no way of hearing the news, Ezekiel received a word from God that was more personal than anything he had been asked to carry before.

"Son of man, with one blow I am about to take away from you the delight of your eyes. Yet do not lament or weep or shed any tears. Groan quietly; do not mourn for the dead. Keep your turban fastened and your sandals on your feet; do not cover your mustache and beard or eat the customary food of mourners." (Ezekiel 24:16–17)

The next verse is one of the most restrained sentences in Scripture: "So I spoke to the people in the morning, and in the evening my wife died. The next morning I did as I had been commanded" (Ezekiel 24:18). This is the only time the Bible mentions her, and we are never told her name. What we are told is how her husband saw her. The Hebrew phrase behind "the delight of your eyes" is machmad 'eneyka, the thing your eyes rest on with longing. It is the language of a man who still looked up when his wife walked into the room.

The customs God forbade were the ordinary signs of grief in ancient Israel. A mourner would take off his turban and sandals, cover the lower part of his face, and sit while others cared for him. The "customary food of mourners" is, in Hebrew, lechem anashim, literally "the bread of men," and many scholars understand it as the meals that neighbors brought to a house of grief. Jeremiah 16:7 describes the same practice, people offering food and drink to console someone who has lost a father or mother. In our terms, Ezekiel was told to send back the pancit. There would be no tent in the street, no cousins at the gate, and no one sitting with him through the night.

The exiles noticed. A priest whose wife had just died was walking around with his turban on and his sandals fastened, and it disturbed them. "Won't you tell us what these things have to do with us?" they asked (Ezekiel 24:19). God's answer came through Ezekiel's lips: "I am about to desecrate my sanctuary, the stronghold in which you take pride, the delight of your eyes, the object of your affection" (Ezekiel 24:21). Soon news would come that the temple had been burned and that the sons and daughters left behind in Jerusalem had died. When it did, the exiles would respond the way Ezekiel had. They would "not mourn or weep but will waste away because of your sins and groan among yourselves" (Ezekiel 24:23). Their grief would be too large, and their shame too heavy, for the ordinary comforts of a wake.

The phrase that keeps this passage from being only harsh is "the delight of your eyes." God used the same words for the temple that he had used for Ezekiel's wife. One way to read this is that the prophet's private loss was a window into God's own heart. The Lord was about to lose a house he loved, the place where he had chosen to dwell among his people, and he was not watching from a cold distance. When he asked Ezekiel to bear this sign, he was asking his servant to feel, in a human body, something of what heaven was feeling over Jerusalem. The command was severe, and it was also strangely intimate. God let Ezekiel stand where he himself stood.

The chapter also refuses to end in silence. Since his calling, Ezekiel had been unable to speak freely except when God gave him a message (Ezekiel 3:26–27). Now God promised that on the day a survivor arrived with news of Jerusalem's fall, "your mouth will be opened; you will speak with him and will no longer be silent" (Ezekiel 24:27). Years later that promise came true. The evening before the messenger reached him, Ezekiel writes, the Lord "opened my mouth before the man came to me in the morning; my mouth was opened and I was no longer silent" (Ezekiel 33:22). From that point his preaching turns toward hope, toward dry bones that live and a new heart for a scattered people. The man who had been made to grieve alone became the voice through whom God spoke comfort to a whole nation.

Ezekiel's lonely obedience was a sign for one terrible season, and the rest of Scripture shows God's ordinary will for his people. Paul tells the church to "mourn with those who mourn" (Romans 12:15). Standing outside the tomb of Lazarus, Jesus wept (John 11:35), even though he knew he would call his friend out of the grave within minutes. The God who once withheld the bread of mourners from his prophet as a warning has, in Christ, come to sit at our wakes himself. Read against that background, every tray of food carried into a house of grief becomes a small picture of the gospel. Grief was never meant to be carried alone, and a plate of pancit carried to a neighbor's lamay is a small, holy way of saying so.

That has two practical edges for us. If someone you know has lost a loved one this month, whether a coworker, a classmate's parent, or the family three houses down, the most faithful thing you can do this week may be simply to show up. You do not need the right words, since the neighbor with the pancit said nothing at all. Bring something, sit for an hour, and come back on a night when the crowd has thinned, because grief tends to grow lonelier after the burial. If you are the one grieving, consider whether you have kept your turban fastened out of pride or a fear of being a burden. God asked that of Ezekiel for a purpose that has already been fulfilled. He does not ask it of you, and the people bringing food to your door are part of his answer to your tears.

The Lord who called a woman "the delight of your eyes" understands what it is to lose what you love. He did not leave his prophet speechless forever, and he will not leave you there either. Tonight, think of one name, someone carrying a loss this season, and decide how you will sit with them before the week is over.

articles.title: The Mother Who Went to Court
articles.dek: An enslaved woman walked into a courtroom to plead for her stolen son. One verse in Psalm 119 asks God to do the same for us, and the Hebrew behind it is more tender than most of us realize.
articles.quote: Before you ever find the words to ask, the One who calls you family has already taken up your case.
articles.illustration: Sojourner Truth wins back her son
articles.body:
In 1827, in the farm country of Ulster County, New York, a tall woman named Isabella learned that her five-year-old son, Peter, had been sold away. She had been born into slavery in that county, and she had only recently walked off the farm of the man who held her, carrying her infant daughter. New York was in the final stretch of ending slavery, and its law forbade selling an enslaved child out of the state. Peter had been sold anyway, passed from one buyer to another until he ended up on a plantation in Alabama. Isabella could not read, and she had no money and no standing. She was a Black woman with no rights the powerful were bound to respect, asking for a child they considered property.

She went anyway. She went to the family responsible, and the mistress of the house laughed at her for making such a fuss over "a little nigger." Isabella answered quietly that she would have her child again. Quaker neighbors pointed her toward the courthouse in Kingston, and she put her case before the grand jury. Years later she described how she felt walking away from that house: "Oh, I felt so tall within, I felt as if the power of a nation was with me." The case dragged on for months, and in 1828 the court ordered Peter brought back from Alabama.

Then came the hardest moment. When the boy was brought into the courtroom, he screamed and clung to the man who had taken him, crying that this woman was not his mother. He had been beaten and frightened into saying it. The judge looked past the terrified child's words, weighed the truth of the matter, and gave Peter back to his mother. Only later, at home, did Isabella find the scars on his back. She would go on to take a new name, Sojourner Truth, and become one of the great voices for freedom in American history. But before any of that, she was simply a mother pleading her son's cause, and winning him home even while he could not yet recognize her.

I have thought about that courtroom often while reading the twentieth stanza of Psalm 119. The psalm is the longest chapter in the Bible, an acrostic poem of twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, with every line in a stanza beginning with the same letter. This section (verses 153 to 160) belongs to the letter resh. By this point the writer has been praying for a long time, and his situation has not improved. "Look on my suffering and deliver me," he begins (Psalm 119:153). A few lines later he admits, "Many are the foes who persecute me" (Psalm 119:157). He is a man under accusation and pressure, surrounded by people who would gladly see him fall, and he has no strength of his own to answer them.

So he asks for an advocate. In the middle of the stanza sits a single line that gathers up everything he needs:

"Defend my cause and redeem me; preserve my life according to your promise." (Psalm 119:154)

Two Hebrew words in that verse open it wide. The first phrase reads literally rivah rivi, "plead my plea" or "argue my lawsuit." The word riv belongs to the courtroom. It is what a lawyer does when he stands up and speaks for a client who cannot speak for himself. The psalmist is asking God to step into the dock beside him and make the argument he cannot make.

The second word is ga'al, "redeem," and it comes from the language of family. In ancient Israel, the go'el was the kinsman redeemer, the closest relative whose duty was to rescue a family member in trouble. If you fell into debt and had to sell your land, the go'el bought it back. If poverty forced you into servitude, he paid your price and brought you home. This is the role Boaz plays for Ruth and Naomi in the book of Ruth. A go'el was never a hired professional. He acted because you were his own.

Put the two words together and the prayer becomes remarkably tender. The psalmist is asking God to be his lawyer and his next of kin at the same time, the One who argues his case in public and the One who loves him as family. Scripture joins these same two ideas elsewhere. Proverbs warns anyone who would cheat orphans by moving their boundary stones: "for their Defender is strong; he will take up their case against you" (Proverbs 23:11). The word translated "Defender" there is go'el, and "take up their case" is the same riv. The orphan has no father to protect him, so God declares himself the family member who will go to court. Jeremiah, writing from the ruins of Jerusalem in Lamentations, looks back and says it has already happened: "You, Lord, took up my case; you redeemed my life" (Lamentations 3:58).

The prayer also has a heartbeat running through it. Three times in these eight verses the psalmist asks God to "preserve my life" (Psalm 119:154, 156, 159). The Hebrew word, chayyeni, means "give me life" or "revive me." Each time, he grounds the request in something different: God's promise, God's laws, and finally God's love. "Your compassion, LORD, is great," he says (Psalm 119:156). He is leaning his whole weight on the character of the One he is calling family.

Isabella's story helps me see what this means for us. She pleaded for a son who, in the crucial moment, did not recognize her. He was too frightened and too wounded to know who was fighting for him, and she brought him home anyway. One way to read Psalm 119:154 in light of the whole Bible is that God's advocacy for us works the same way. The New Testament says plainly that "we have an advocate with the Father" (1 John 2:1), and Paul writes that Christ Jesus "is at the right hand of God and is also interceding for us" (Romans 8:34). Our Redeemer does his pleading on our behalf even on the days when we feel far from him, when we are too tired or too ashamed to pray, or when the voices around us have convinced us we belong to someone else. Before you ever find the words to ask, the One who calls you family has already taken up your case.

Many Filipinos know what it is to stand without a defender. Perhaps you work abroad for an employer who holds your passport and your wages, or perhaps someone at the office has twisted your words and the story about you is already spreading. Perhaps the accusing voice is your own, replaying an old failure late at night. In any of those places, this verse gives you a prayer you can pray in a single breath. You can say it on the jeepney, at your desk, or lying awake: "Lord, plead my case and bring me home." You are allowed to hand over the argument you cannot win to the One who argues for you as family.

The stanza ends with the line that made all of the psalmist's hope possible: "All your words are true; all your righteous laws are eternal" (Psalm 119:160). The Hebrew opens with rosh, a word meaning "head" or "sum," so the verse can be read, "The sum of your word is truth." Isabella's judge looked past a frightened boy's words to the larger truth of the case. God does the same with you. The lies spoken over you, and even the ones you have believed, will not have the last word in his court.

Today, if there is a situation where you feel unheard or misjudged, write Psalm 119:154 on a small card and keep it where you will see it. Each time it catches your eye, let it remind you that your case is already in good hands. You have a Defender who is strong, a Redeemer who calls you his own, and a Father who will bring you home.

articles.title: The Door Manila Opened
articles.dek: In the late 1930s, a Philippine president made room for Jewish families most of the world had turned away. Proverbs 24 explains why God never accepts the excuse "we didn't know."
articles.quote: Rescued people are the ones God sends to hold back the staggering.
articles.illustration: Quezon's Open Doors for Jewish refugees
articles.body:
In July 1938, delegates from thirty-two nations met in the French resort town of Évian to talk about the Jewish families trying to escape Nazi Germany. Over several polite days, one country after another explained why it could take only a few refugees, or none at all. Families in Vienna and Berlin read the newspapers and understood that most of the world's doors were closing. Meanwhile, in Manila, a city most Europeans could not have found on a map, a small group of people was already deciding to answer differently.

The Frieder brothers were American Jews who ran a cigar business in Manila, and they began asking whether the Philippines might take in refugees. They found a willing listener in President Manuel L. Quezon. With help from the American High Commissioner, Paul McNutt, and a young military officer then serving in Manila named Dwight Eisenhower, they built a quiet system for issuing visas. Between 1937 and 1941, about 1,300 Jewish men, women, and children escaped Europe and started over in the Philippines. Quezon gave land of his own in Marikina, where Marikina Hall was built in 1940 to house refugee families, and plans to settle thousands more in Mindanao ended only because the war arrived first.

Quezon had critics, and the Commonwealth was a poor country with troubles of its own. When he dedicated Marikina Hall in April 1940, he answered them by saying he hoped the Filipino people would one day be glad that, when the time of need came, their country had been willing to extend a hand of welcome. In 2017 a monument called "Open Doors" was unveiled in Rishon LeZion, Israel, to thank the Philippines. Some of the children who came through Manila lived long lives and told their grandchildren that their story began again on Philippine soil. Quezon and his friends saw people being led away, and they decided that knowing was reason enough to act.

Nearly three thousand years earlier, a teacher in Israel wrote about that same moment of decision. Proverbs 24:10–14 sits inside a section the book calls "sayings of the wise" (Proverbs 22:17), a collection of about thirty short teachings, written in the voice of a father training a son for public life. Scholars have long noticed that parts of this section resemble an older Egyptian teaching called the Instruction of Amenemope, which suggests Israel's wise men knew the wisdom of their neighbors. They took the best of it and placed it under the authority of the God of Israel. Our passage reads like a single conversation between that father and his son about courage, responsibility, and hope.

The father begins with a hard sentence: "If you falter in a time of trouble, how small is your strength!" (Proverbs 24:10). Then he paints a picture his first readers would have recognized from the ancient world, where prisoners and captives were marched in lines toward execution. "Rescue those being led away to death; hold back those staggering toward slaughter" (Proverbs 24:11). The word for "staggering" describes people who are tottering and stumbling, too weak to walk straight. The son can see them. And the father knows exactly what a comfortable person says when a crisis is inconvenient, so he answers the excuse before it is spoken.

"If you say, 'But we knew nothing about this,' does not he who weighs the heart perceive it? Does not he who guards your life know it? Will he not repay everyone according to what they have done?" (Proverbs 24:12)

In Hebrew, verse 10 contains a small wordplay that English cannot carry. The word for "trouble" is tsarah, and the word for "small" is tsar, which means narrow or tight. A fair way to hear it is this: in the day of narrowness, your strength turns out to be narrow. Trouble does not create our smallness. It reveals how small our hearts already were. The father is gently telling his son that the real test of strength comes on the day someone else is in danger and helping them will cost something.

Verse 12 then names two things about God. He is the one "who weighs the heart," a phrase Proverbs uses elsewhere too: "all a person's ways seem pure to them, but motives are weighed by the LORD" (Proverbs 16:2). Egyptians pictured a dead person's heart being weighed on scales after death, and Israel's teachers borrowed the image to say that the true God weighs us now, in the middle of our choices. Yet the second title is even more tender. He is also the one "who guards your life." The same God who sees through our excuses is the God who has been keeping us alive every single day. One way to read the verse is as a reminder that every breath we have is guarded by Someone else, so we are in no position to shrug at another person's danger.

This is where the passage opens onto the gospel. Before we were ever rescuers, we were the ones in the line. Paul says it plainly: "You see, at just the right time, when we were still powerless, Christ died for the ungodly" (Romans 5:6). We were the staggering ones, too weak to walk out of the line on our own. And God did the very thing Proverbs 24:11 commands. Isaiah describes the coming Servant with words that echo our passage: "he was led like a lamb to the slaughter" (Isaiah 53:7). Jesus stepped into the line of those being led away to death so that we could be held back from it. He saw us, he knew, and he came.

That changes how we hear the father's warning. The command to rescue is the natural response of people who have already been rescued. Quezon's Manila became a refuge because a few people decided a stranger's survival was their business. Christians have a deeper reason than he did. The God who guards our lives once reached into the line and pulled us out, and he now sends us back toward others who are stumbling. Rescued people are the ones God sends to hold back the staggering.

Most of us will never sign visas for a thousand refugees. But the people staggering near us are usually close enough to touch. It may be a cousin abroad who stopped answering messages, a co-worker whose drinking has quietly grown worse, a teenager in the family who seems to be disappearing into a screen, or a neighbor drowning in loans from five different lenders. The easiest thing in the world is to tell ourselves we did not really know. Proverbs gently removes that option. God weighs the heart, and he sees that most of the time we knew enough to make one phone call, ask one honest question, or offer one practical kindness.

The father then ends his teaching with something sweet. "Eat honey, my son, for it is good; honey from the comb is sweet to your taste. Know also that wisdom is like honey for you: If you find it, there is a future hope for you, and your hope will not be cut off" (Proverbs 24:13–14). After a hard word about responsibility, he reminds his son that wisdom is a delight to taste. A life spent noticing and helping others leads somewhere good, toward a future that God promises to protect.

Today, ask the Lord to bring to mind one person who seems to be stumbling, and then do one small, concrete thing for them before the day ends. Send the message, buy the meal, sit with them, or simply say, "I noticed, and I am here." Your strength may feel narrow, but the God who guards your life will supply what you lack. You were carried out of the line by Someone who loved you, and he is glad to make you part of someone else's rescue story.
